titleStmt.title: Schedulability Analysis of GMF-Modeled Messages over Controller Area Networks with Mixed-Queues

analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis of GMF-Modeled Messages over Controller Area Networks with Mixed-Queues

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Controller Area Network (CAN) is widely utilized in many industrial real-time applications. As a real-time communication network, the predictability of timing behaviors is very important. Therefore, many works have been proposed regarding the schedulability analysis of CAN messages. Most of the existing analysis approaches are based on a traditional periodic message model. However, in some applications, the transmission of a message may follow a certain pattern instead of repeating the same transmission period by period. In these cases, applying the existing analysis methods may lead to quite pessimistic results. In order to tackle this problem, in this paper we apply the Generalized Multi-Frame (GMF) task model on CAN messages, where both priority-based and FIFO-based message queues are taken into account. We present a corresponding sufficient schedulability analysis. According to the experimental evaluations, our analysis can provide tighter results compared to the existing CAN message response time analysis in the context of GMF-modeled messages.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The Controller Area Network (CAN) [1] is one of the most well-known real-time communication networks, which has been utilized in many different areas in industry. Generally, the messages in a network are associated with unique identifiers which are considered as their fixed priorities. The transmission over a CAN bus employs a priority-based arbitration scheme. These messages are generated by tasks located on different nodes called Electronic Control Units (ECU).

div.head: A. Motivation and Contribution
div.p: As a real-time communication network, the predictability of CAN messages is very important in order to guarantee the safety and reliability. Therefore, many works have been proposed regarding the schedulability analysis of CAN messages. Most of the existing methods assume the traditional periodic message model, where there is only one instance of a message in each period and the transmission of this instance is repeated period by period. As we mentioned above, the messages are generated by tasks. Therefore, if tasks are following a periodic model, the corresponding messages can also be considered as periodic. However, as discussed in [2] [3], sometimes the generations of tasks are repeated following a specific pattern where in each cycle there can be several different instances. For these applications, it is difficult to apply the traditional periodic model. Consequently, if the CAN messages under analysis are generated by this type of tasks, we cannot simply use the existing analysis methods due to the incompatibility with the assumed message model. Therefore, in this paper, we apply the Generalized Multi-Frame (GMF) model [3] on CAN messages with arbitrary deadlines, and present a corresponding guaranteed schedulability analysis. In the evaluation phase, a number of experiments have been generated, where we aim to examine the difference between our analysis and the existing analysis method considering the GMF-modeled messages. Moreover, in order to show the scalability and applicability, we also examine the computation time of our analysis from the experiments.

div.head: B. Related Work
div.p: The first response-time based schedulability analysis of CAN messages is presented by Tindell et al. in [4], which is based on the task response-time analysis presented in [5]. In [6], Davis et al. presented a revised schedulability analysis, where the potential optimism in [4] is removed. Based on these works, some other analysis methods have also been proposed regarding different system features. In [7], the authors take into account different initial phases (i.e. offsets) of messages in the analysis. In [8] [9], the authors present the analysis for mixed-queued messages, where some ECUs use priority-based message queues and the others use First-In-First-Out (FIFO) based message queues. Later on in [10], the authors extend the analysis presented in [7] and [8] to support both time-triggered and event-triggered messages. Many other analysis approaches regarding CAN messages have also been published, however, most of them are based on the traditional periodic message model.

The Multi-Frame (MF) task model was first presented in [2], which is a generalization of the traditional periodic task model [11]. In the MF model, tasks are released periodically based on large cycles. Within one large cycle, there can be several different instances (i.e. with different worstcase execution times), but the minimum inter-arrival times between successive instances are identical. This model is further generalized in [3], where the minimum inter-arrival times between successive instances within one large cycle can be different. Some schedulability analysis for the MF and GMF modeled tasks have been proposed, such as [12] [13] [3]. Unfortunately, these analysis methods always focus on preemptive task scheduling, which cannot be directly applied on CAN messages especially when we consider both prioritybased and FIFO-based message queues.

In our previous work [14], we present a sufficient responsetime-based schedulability analysis for MF-modeled CAN messages. The applicability of that analysis is limited due to the assumptions of constraint deadlines and the satisfaction of the Accumulative Monotonic (AM) property. In this paper, we present the schedulability of more generalized CAN messages (i.e. GMF modeled) with arbitrary deadlines, and the assumption of the AM property is also removed. We also provide some experimental evaluation, where we compare our analysis with the existing analysis method regarding GMF-modeled CAN messages.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we briefly introduce the system model and the GMF model used in this paper. In Section III, we illustrate the details of our response-time based schedulability analysis. Some results of our experiments are shown in Section IV. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and brings some thoughts about our future work.

div.head: A. System Model
div.p: In this paper, the analyzed system comprises a number of ECUs and a shared CAN bus. Similar to [8], an ECU can use a priority-based message queue or a FIFO-based message queue. Once a task on an ECU generates a message frame, this frame will be delivered to the local message queue. When a frame becomes the head of the corresponding message queue, it will enter the bus-arbitration competing with the head frames queued on other ECUs. Only the frame, who succeeds in the bus-arbitration (i.e. it has the highest priority among all the competitors within this arbitration round), can complete its transmission.

div.head: B. Generalized Multi-Frame Model
div.p: The traditional periodic task model is introduced by Liu & Layland in [11], where each task is characterized by a certain worst-case execution time and a specific period. This model has been utilized to model CAN messages in many existing works. However, if we want to model a message which repeatedly generates a frame sequence instead of a single frame, this model may not be appropriate.

In order to model a task whose execution times change periodically based on a specific pattern, in [2], the authors introduced the Multi-Frame (MF) task model. In [3], the MF model was further extended to the Generalized Multi-Frame (GMF) model. A schedulability analysis for CAN messages with the MF model has been proposed in [14]. In the MF model, the variations are only allowed for the sizes of different frames of the same message, but not for the minimum separation times. However, in the GMF model, the variations can also occur on minimum inter-arrival times, which can obviously increase the corresponding applicability. Therefore, in this paper, we try to model CAN messages with the GMF model.
Under the GMF model, a multi-frame message can be characterized as

The array -→ C i = {C i,1 ,C i,2 , ...,C i,N i } represents the transmission times of the N i sequential frames within one large cycle. Similarly, -→ T i = {T i,1 , T i,2 , ..., T i,N i } contains the corresponding minimum inter-arrival times between successive frames. Note that the subscripts refer to the corresponding frames. The release jitter J i represents the maximum time interval between the arrival and the release of a frame. Typically, a CAN bus employs a priority-based arbitration mechanism, where the priority of each message (denoted by P i ) is associated with its unique IDentifier (ID). A lower ID always denotes a higher priority. The above message parameters are illustrated in Fig. 1-b. div.head: III. WORST-CASE TRANSMISSION DELAY ANALYSIS A. Maximum Interference Function
div.p: As presented in [6], the basic idea of response time analysis of CAN messages is to compute the requested transmission time of related messages within a time interval (i.e. a busy period). In [14], the authors utilize a function to compute the cumulative requested transmission time of an MF-modeled message within a certain time interval. However, that function is not applicable for the analysis of GMF-modeled messages, due to the variation of minimum inter-arrival times within one large cycle. Therefore, first of all, we need to redesign the computation of the maximum cumulative requested transmission time of a GMF message.

In Algorithm 1, we present the calculation of the maximum cumulative transmission request of message M i under a given time duration t, where the first arrived frame is the k th frame F i,k . Regarding the length of t, the calculation can be divided into three possible cases.

a) Case 1: t is larger than the large cycle of M i The arrivals of M i is repeated every large cycle, so t can be divided into two parts (i.e. t nT and t rest ). The first part t nT is an integer multiple of the large cycle of M i (i.e. line 1 and 3). The second part is the remaining time duration in t, which is computed by line 4. The cumulative transmission request in one large cycle is fixed, which is the sum of transmission times of all the frames in one large cycle. Therefore, the cumulative transmission request of t nT can be computed by line 2.

Due to the repeated transmission, the first arrived frame in t rest should be the same as F i,k , and its arrival time is supposed to be at the beginning of t rest . Then the cumulative transmission time request of the second part (i.e. C rest ) can be increased frame by frame, until the end of t rest (line 6 to 17). Note that, according to the above discussion, if t rest = 0, the time interval t should be terminated just before the arrival of a following frame of M i . In order to provide guaranteed results, we should take this newly arrived frame into account in C rest .
Finally, the total cumulative transmission time request of M i within t can be computed by the sum of C nT and C rest .

b) Case 2: t is equal to the large cycle of M i This case can be considered as a special case of Case 1, where n T = 1, and t rest = 0. Therefore, C rest = C i,k , and we only need to compute C nT (i.e. line 2). c) Case 3: t is less the large cycle of M i This case is also a special case of Case 1, where t nT = 0, and t rest = t. Therefore, only C rest needs to be computed (line line 6 to 18).

Regarding different initial frames, each message can have N i possible arrival patterns (i.e. called sequences hereinafter). In other words, a message N i can be characterized in N i ways (see Example 2).
Example 2. In Example 1, M i can have three possible sequences, which can be described as {{3,1,2}, {4,5,6}, {10,10,10}, 0, 1}, {{1,2,3}, {5,6,4}, 10, 0, 1} and {{2,3,1}, {6,4,5}, {10,10,10}, 0, 1}.

As presented in [2] [14], if a multi-frame message can satisfy the Accumulative Monotonic (AM) property, we can find out the critical sequence of this message which can lead to the worst-case cumulative transmission time request. However, the AM property is quite limited which may not be meaningful for real industry applications. On another hand, if we implement an exhaustive search on all the possibilities (i.e. try all the possible values of k for each message), the computation time of the whole analysis will be increased sharply as the number of messages goes up. This may also not be acceptable due to the limitation of the computing resource in reality. Therefore, we aim to create a single function for each message, which can provide its maximum cumulative transmission time request without dependencies on the input information k. In other words, given a time interval t, we aim to determine which sequence of M i can cause its maximum cumulative transmission request. In Algorithm 2, we create a matrix which contains the cumulative transmission requests for all the possible sequences within one large cycle.

As described in our message model, the transmission is repeated every large cycle, which is independent of the initial frame. Consequently, no matter which frame of M i arrives first in the given time duration, we only need to focus on one single large cycle. Apparently, we only need to analyze at the time instants when there can be a change of the cumulative transmission request of M i . Therefore, first we need to create a list of check-points CPL (line 1 to 6 in Algorithm 2). We define a check-point as a time instant when there is a newly arrived frame of M i . At each check-point, the cumulative transmission requests of M i can be increased. Assume that the first frame of M i arrives at time 0, in order to get the maximum cumulative transmission requests, all the following frames should arrive as early as possible (line 4 in Algorithm 2). As discussed above, we need to check all the N i sequences to provide guarantees

div.p: end for 13: end for 14: return CT RM (line 2 to 5 in Algorithm 2). After resorting and removing duplicated items (line 6 in Algorithm 2), the check-points list CPL contains all the time instants, when there can be increases of cumulative transmission requests, within a large cycle. Moreover, the last item of CPL is supposed to be equal to the large cycle.

For each possible arrival sequence of M i , the cumulative transmission requests can be computed by Eq. 1, where the input time intervals are all the check-points in CPL (line 7 to 13 in Algorithm 2). In order to represent the checkpoints and corresponding cumulative transmission requests, we can create a matrix CT RM (i.e. Cumulative Transmission Request Matrix). The first row is the check-points from CPL (line 8 in Algorithm 2) and each other row contains the corresponding cumulative transmission requests for a specific arrival sequence. In other words, in each column, the first item is a check-point, and the other items are the computed cumulative transmission requests at this check-point regarding different arrival sequences. This process is an exhaustive process. Therefore, using Algorithm 2, we can create a matrix CT RM (also denoted as CT RM i ), from which we can find the cumulative transmission requests caused by all possible sequences of M i at each check-point.
Then we can see that, given a time duration [0, 6], these three sequences can respectively provide 4, 3 and 5 time units of cumulative transmission requests.

For the first solution, we can simply just keep the maximum cumulative transmission request at each check-point from CT RM i . Then we can get a two-dimensional matrix (denoted as CT RM i ) which consists of all the check-points and corresponding maximum cumulative request. Given a time duration t, the new matrix can provide a guaranteed cumulative transmission request of M i , but it may include pessimism. First, let us think about the source of the input time duration t. As mentioned in [14], the response time of a frame includes blocking delay (i.e. caused by lower priority messages), interference delay (caused by higher priority messages) and its own transmission delay. Similar to Eq. 6 in [14], we aim to iteratively compute the interference delay that M i can cause to other messages. Therefore, as t increases exceeding a certain check-point, we need to take the cumulative transmission request of M i before that check-point into account for the next iteration. At a certain check-point, one sequence may incur the maximum cumulative transmission request, but at the previous check-point, this sequence may cause much less transmission request than some others. In other words, sometimes the time duration t may reach a certain check-point pt only based on a specific arrival sequence, but at pt, the maximum value in CT RM is caused by another sequence. In this case, we cannot simply use the observed maximum value, because actually the calculation based on the sequence of this value cannot reach pt (see Example 4). Assume that the message under analysis is message M j , which may get interference from message M i and some other messages. According to the traditional response time analysis [6], the total interference time (i.e. denoted by t) is a busy period (i.e. no bus idle time within this time interval) between the end of the blocking interval (caused by lower priority messages) and the start of the transmission of M j . This busy period consists of two parts. One part is the transmission time of message other than M i within t (denoted as CT R others (t)), and the other part is the transmission time of M i within t (denoted as CT R M i (t)). Assume that CT R others (t) is given as a fixed value, then t can be changed together with CT R M i (t) (i.e. they influence each other). As presented in [6], the response time analysis is based on an iterative calculation until a convergence is observed. For simplicity, in this example, we assume that the blocking delay of M j is 0. Once the computation of the response time of a certain frame converges, the included interference time will also become stable since the transmission time of the analyzed frame is fixed. In other words, we aim to iteratively compute a convergence value of t. Now we assume that CT R others (t) = 2 and t = 0 at the beginning.
div.formula: Iteration 1: t = CT R others (0) +CT R M i (0) = 2 + 3 = 5 Iteration 2: t = CT R others (5) +CT R M i (5) = 2 + 4 = 6 Iteration 3: t = CT R others (6) +CT R M i (6) = 2 + 5 = 7 Iteration 4: t = CT R others (7) +CT R M i (7) = 2 + 5 = 7
div.p: The converged time duration t is 7 which means the corresponding cumulative transmission request of M i is 5. However, actually when CT R others is 2, the busy time interval t can only reach 6 but never 7. As shown in Figure 2, no matter how we start the transmissions, the maximum value of the busy duration t is 6.

The main reason of the pessimism is that at different checkpoints, the maximum cumulative transmission requests may be caused by different sequences. For example, in the CT RM i of the above example, the maximum cumulative transmission request of M i before time instant 6 is caused by the first sequence. However, at time instant 6, the maximum cumulative transmission request is caused by the third sequence. Then the problem comes because if the calculation is based on the third sequence from the beginning, t cannot reach time instant 6 at all. As the number of messages in the network goes up, the pessimism of the whole analysis can become very high. Therefore, we need to capture this feature in the analysis to reduce pessimism.

The basic idea of our tighter analysis 2 is to trace the maximum cumulative transmission request regarding the increase of check-points. If the largest cumulative transmission requests are caused by the same sequence from the beginning, then we just simply add them (i.e. each check-point and the corresponding observed maximum cumulative transmission request) into a new matrix (denoted as MCT RM). However, at a certain point (called cp y ), if the maximum cumulative transmission request is caused by another sequence (called s 2 ) rather than the sequence (called s 1 ) which caused the largest request at the previous check-point (called cp x ), we need to compensate the difference of cumulative requests at cp x between s 1 and s 2 . The compensation is achieved by introducing a postponed phase to the cumulative transmission request of s 2 at cp y (see Lemma 1).

Therefore, while creating a complete MCT RM, we need to assume that t is always large enough to reach all the check-points in CT RM. As we mentioned above, t includes the transmission time of other messages and the transmission time of M i . Assume the transmission time of other messages is ∆t, which is a non-decreasing function of t and can be determined by the transmission request at the previous checkpoint. Therefore, we know that ∆t 1,x ≥ ∆t 2,x . div.p: As we discussed above, when we create MCT RM, we only pick the maximum cumulative transmission request at each check-point. In other words, at cp x , we assume the transmission request of M i to be t 1,x but not t 2,x . As shown in Eq. 2, after cp x , the time interval t is no less than cp y + (t 1,xt 2,x ).

On the other hand, if we assume that t 1,x + ∆t 1,x < cp y + (t 1,xt 2,x ), we have t 2,x + ∆t 2,x < cp y . In this case, the time interval t can never reach cp y through s 2 , which means that we cannot get the cumulative request of t 2,y .

In this case, we can get two possible situations, cp y + (t 1,xt 2,x ) > cp z or cp y + (t 1,xt 2,x ) ≤ cp z . In the former situation, we also have to postpone the request caused by s 2 at cp z . In this case, the calculation is based on the difference between t 1,y (caused at cp y ) and t 2,x (caused at cp x ), because t 2,y has already been postponed after cp z . Similarly, in the worst-case, we have to re-calculate the postponed phases at all the following checkpoints (including newly add check-points due to the compensation, such as cp y +(t 1,x -t 2,x )), the algorithm will become very complex. In CT RM, the cumulative transmission requests for each sequence are monotonically increased as the check-points go up. Therefore, an upper-bounded postponement, which is shorter than a complete postponed phase, cannot cause any optimism. In order to decrease the complexity of the algorithm, we bound the postponed phase by cp zcp y . In other words, the request t 2,y at cp y cannot be delayed later than cp z . Then it becomes the same as the latter situation.

As we mentioned before, the cumulative requests can only change at the check-points in CPL. As a result, under the latter situation, at cp y + (t 1,xt 2,x ), which is between cp y and cp z , there is no increase of the cumulative request of any sequence. Therefore, the postponement at cp y will not affect the checking process at cp z .
Consequently, to achieve the cumulative transmission request t 2,y , the corresponding check-point can be changed from cp y to min(cp z , cp y + (t 1,xt 2,x )).

According to the above discussion, we can create the MCT RM of M i by finding the maximum cumulative transmission request at each check-point step by step. Finally, MCT RM i will be a two-dimensional matrix, which consists of all check-points within a large cycle of M i and the corresponding maximum cumulative transmission requests.

div.head: B. Priority-Queued Messages
div.p: In [6], the authors have presented the schedulability analysis for priority-queued CAN messages with arbitrary deadlines. In this subsection, we extend their analysis to support GMFmodelled CAN messages.

As presented in [8] and [9], a frame F i,k of a message in a FIFO queue may experience a bounded buffering time before it enters the priority-based bus-arbitration. This buffering time can be considered as an extra jitter (denoted by f i,k ), which will be computed in the next section.

According to [6], for traditional periodic messages in priority queues, the worst-case response times can be calculated by examining the response times of all the instances within a critical busy period, where the analyzed message is released together with all the other messages with higher priorities at the beginning of the busy period. The first frames of these messages are assumed to be subject to their maximum jitters, and all the following frames are released as early as possible. Unlike traditional periodic messages, for GMF modelled messages, the maximum sizes of frames from the same message may not be identical. As a result, for different arrival sequences of the analyzed message, the critical busy periods can be different. In other words, we need to take into account all the possible sequences of the message under analysis. Therefore, we can compute the worst-case response time of M i as
div.formula: R i = N i max k=1 r i,k(4)
div.p: where r i,k represents the worst-case response time of M i when the first arrived frame of M i in the critical busy period is F i,k . On another hand, for the messages rather than the analyzed message M i , we do not need to consider different sequences due to the use of Eq. 3 (i.e. all the sequences have been taken into account while we create MCT RMs).

CAN employs a non-preemptive transmission mechanism, which means that once a frame starts to be transmitted, it cannot be preempted by any other frames even if those other frames have higher priorities. This kind of buffering time of M i , which is caused by lower priority messages, is called blocking time [6]. Similar to [6], we just need to find the maximum-sized frame of messages with lower priorities than M i . Therefore, the blocking term can be bounded by
div.formula: B i = max j∈l p(M i ) ( N i max p=1 C j,p )(5)
div.p: where l p(M i ) denotes the set of messages whose priorities are lower than the priority of M i .

In [9], the authors use a fixed point equation (i.e. Eq. 4 in [9]) to calculate the time duration (in this paper denoted by w i,k (q), where F i,k is the first arrived frame of M i ) from the beginning of the busy period to the start of the transmission of the analyzed frame (denoted by frame F i,k+q ). Assume that q denotes the index of the frame under analysis, and q = 0 refers to the first frame of the analyzed message within the busy period. This time duration consists of three factors: the blocking delay, which is caused by the transmission of lower priority messages; the transmission times of the frames of M i , which are ahead of the analyzed frame; the interference delay, which is caused by the transmission of messages with higher priorities.

As presented above, the blocking delay can be bounded by Eq. 5. Given the first arrived frame of M i , we can also bound the transmission time of frames of M i which are ahead of the analyzed frame by

div.p: The calculation of interference delay in [9] is valid based on the condition that the minimum inter-arrival times between frames of the same message are given as an identical value (i.e. periods in the traditional periodic message model). However, in the GMF model, the minimum inter-arrival times between frames may vary, which means that we cannot simply apply the solution presented in [9]. The basic idea behind computing the interference delay is to examine the number of arrivals of messages whose priorities are higher than the priority of the analyzed message within the busy period. This is exactly what we have presented in the previous subsection. Therefore, we can use Eq. 3 to compute interference delay.

div.head: C. FIFO-Queued Messages
div.p: In this subsection, we present the analysis for FIFO-queued messages with arbitrary deadlines. A FIFO-queued frame F i,k can not be transmitted until all the frames, which enter the queue earlier than F i,k , finish their transmissions, even if F i,k has the highest priority.

Basically, the difference between the analysis of priorityqueued and FIFO-queued messages is the extra buffering time of FIFO-queued messages before entering bus-arbitration (i.e. bus-arbitration is always priority-based). Therefore, as mentioned in [9], comparing to priority-queued messages, the time duration w i,k (q) for a FIFO-queued message M i consists of one more factor, which is the interference delay (denoted by I i,k (q, w n i,k )) from the messages within the same ECU transmitted prior to the analyzed frame of M i .

Moreover, in order to provide guaranteed results, we always assume the worst-case scenarios. All the messages in the MS(M i ) (which denotes the message set where all the messages are generated from the same ECU as the source of M i ) are transmitted at the lowest priority (denoted by L M i ) of any message in this message set [9]. In other words, M i may get interference from a message (generated by another ECU) with a priority higher than L M i , even if the priority of this message is lower than the priority of M i .
According to the above discussion, the maximum time duration from the start of the busy period to the analyzed frame (F i,k+q ) beginning its transmission can be computed by
div.formula: w n+1 i,k (q) = B i +C ahead i,k + I i,k (q, w n i,k ) + ∑ j∈hp(L M i ) ∧ j ∈MS(M i ) δ j (w n i,k + J j + f j + τ bit )(11)
div.p: where F i,k is the first arrived frame of M i within the busy period. B i is computed by Eq. 5, and C ahead i,k is given by Eq. 7. If M j is a priority-queued message, we set f j = 0.

Considering the worst-case scenario, while computing the buffering time I i,k (q, w n i,k ), we assume that all the frames of other messages in MS(M i ) are released ahead of the analyzed frame of M i . Therefore, this buffering time can be given by
div.formula: I i,k (q, w n i,k ) = ∑ j∈MS(M i ) ∧M j =M i δ j (w n i,k + J j + τ bit )(12)
div.p: Then, similar to Eq. 8, the calculation of Eq. 11 can be started with w 0 i,k (q) = B i +C ahead i,k (q). The iteration terminates when w n+1 i,k (q) = w n i,k (q), or when J i + w n+1 i,k (q) -T ahead i,k (q) + C i,k+q > D i,k . The outer calculation begins with q = 0, and ends when J i + w n+1 i,k (q) +C i,k+q < T ahead i,k (q + 1). The response time of a FIFO-queued frame F i,k+q can also be computed by
div.formula: r i,k (q) = J i + w i,k (q) -T ahead i,k (q) +C i,k+q(13)

The upper bound of this jitter can be given by

div.head: D. Schedulability Test
div.p: A circular dependency problem may occur, if messages in different FIFO queues have interleaved priorities (see the example in [8]). Fortunately, we notice that Eq. 4 and Eq. 15 are monotonically non-decreasing regarding the buffering times (i.e. f j ). On another hand, Eq. 16 is also monotonically nondecreasing regarding the response time R j which is computed by Eq. 15. Therefore, as shown in Algorithm 4, we can utilize a similar approach presented in [9], that is to iteratively compute the response time R j for each message M j until the buffering time f j reaches a convergence (i.e. the boolean variable repeat in Algorithm 4 stays as f alse). Based on the outer loop calculation (line 3-22), we can compute upper bounds for the worst-case transmission delays of all messages in the network. The algorithm can be terminated, once the response time of a message exceeds its deadline (line 8-10 or line 17-19), in which case the network is considered as unschedulable. Due to the pessimism involved in the computation, this schedulability analysis is a sufficient but not necessary test.

div.head: IV. EVALUATION
div.p: As we mentioned above, applying the existing schedulability analysis, which assumes a periodic message model, on GMF-modeled messages may result in too much pessimism. In the following subsection, we present some simulationbased experimental results to show the difference between our analysis and the existing approach regarding GMF-modeled messages. Then we show the computation time of our analysis regarding different numbers of messages.

div.head: A. Experiment Settings
div.p: The network in our experiment consists of four ECUs (i.e. E 1 , E 2 , E 3 , and E 4 ), where E 1 and E 4 are equipped with FIFO-based message queues and the rest ECUs use priority-based message queues. The number of frames of each message (i.e. N i ) within one large cycle is randomly selected within [1,5]. The data size of each frame is randomly selected within the range of [3,8] bytes. We assume that all the frames have their maximum stuffing-bits. The large cycle of each message (i.e. T i ) is selected from (20000, 50000, 100000, 200000, 500000, 1000000)µs. The jitter (i.e. J i ) is randomly selected within [0, T i ] and the deadline is selected within [ T i , 2 T i ]. The priority (i.e. ID) of each message is randomly assigned. Moreover, the bus speed is assumed to be 500 kbit/s.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: In this subsection, we compare our analysis with the existing analysis presented in [9] with respect of GMF-modeled messages. of all, in order to apply the analysis in [9], we need to transform GMF-modeled messages into traditional periodic messages. Basically, a GMF-modeled message M i can be transformed into N i messages. Each frame of M i within one large cycle is considered into a separate periodic message, where the period equates to T i . The other parameters (i.e. D i , J i , P i ) are kept the same as M i . Note that the initial phases between the frames of the same message are known, however, the initial phases between different messages are not given. As a result, when we transform a GMF-modeled messages into periodic messages, we cannot simply assign offsets to the created messages. In order to provide guaranteed results, we need to assume the worst-case condition that all the messages are able to release at the same time. This is why the existing approach can cause much pessimism while analyzing GMFmodeled messages.

In these experiments, the number of messages are randomly selected within the range (5, 70). The results are shown in Figure 4. We can get the same observation as the discussion above, that our analysis includes much less pessimism than the existing approach while analyzing GMF-modeled messages. Under our experimental settings, the schedulability according to the existing approach drops sharply (i.e. the dashed line) as the utilization goes up from 0.1 to around 0.4, then the message sets become always unschedulable. On another hand, the schedulability based on our analysis goes down more slowly (i.e. the solid line), and message sets become unschedulable when the total utilization exceeds 0.6. Besides the above transformation model, we also implemented another transformation solution where each GMFmodeled message is converted into a single traditional periodic message. In order to provide a safe transformation, the frame size of the new message equates to the maximum frame size of the original GMF-modeled message, and the period of the new message is equal to the minimum inter-arrival time between the frames of the original message. Unfortunately, the schedulability of the new message set under this transformation solution is very low. The main reason is that the utilization of the message set after transformation may become too high. When the frame sizes and inter-arrival times of a GMF-modeled message varies a lot, the transmission time of the largest frame may be close to the minimum inter-arrival time. In this case, the utilization of the transformed message may become much higher than the original message. As a result, the utilization of the whole message set may become very high, which decreases the schedulability of the network.

div.head: C. Computation Time
div.p: In order to examine the scalability of our analysis, we also measured the computation time of our analysis in the experiments. In these experiments, the total utilization of each message set is selected from (0.3, 0.4, 0.5). We gradually increase the number of messages in the network, and for each given number, we randomly generate 100 experiments. The average computation times regarding different numbers of messages are listed in Table I. As shown in the results, when the number of messages is lower than 100, the average computation time is always less than 3 seconds. As the number of messages goes up, the computation time increases gradually. We do not examine extreme high number of messages, since it may not be necessary for most industrial control systems. For example, in a typical sole body network of a vehicle, the number of messages is just around 60-80 [15].

div.head: V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS
div.p: In this paper, we apply the Generalized Multi-Frame (GMF) task model on CAN messages, and present a corresponding sufficient schedulability analysis. This work is a generalization of our previous work [14]. Some unrealistic assumptions used in [14] have been removed in this paper. The new analysis can support GMF-modeled CAN messages with arbitrary deadlines, where the nodes in the network can have FIFO-based or priority-based message queues. A number of experiments have been generated. Comparing to the existing analysis approach which assumes a periodic message model, our analysis provides tighter results while analyzing GMFmodeled messages. Moreover, we also show the computation time of our analysis in the experiments regarding different numbers of messages.

As mentioned above, the analysis in this paper is sufficient but not necessary due to the pessimism. In order to improve the applicability of our analysis, we need to further reduce the pessimism. Moreover, in this paper, the messages are assumed to have arbitrary priorities. We will think about finding an optimized priority assignment scheme for GMFmodeled messages in our future work.
